input.summary: The claim is nondirectional: adding 20 ms delay "changes" TCP flow completion time under fixed emulated bottleneck conditions. A single emulated pilot can measure whether a difference is observed between 0 ms and 20 ms delay conditions, but cannot prove causality or generalize to all Internet users. Three clarifications are needed before a frozen protocol can be produced.
clarification_questions: Which runner script should be used — netem_nines.py (exactly 2 clients) or netem_cubic_benchmark_nines.py (1–10 clients) — and how many clients per configuration?
What bottleneck link rate (Mbit/s), buffer size (kbytes), file size(s) (MBytes), and CCA(s) should be used for the emulated conditions?
Should the 20 ms delay be applied as a one-way client-to-bottleneck delay or as a round-trip delay, and should loss_pct remain 0?

proposal.problem: It is unknown whether adding 20 ms of emulated network delay measurably changes TCP flow completion time under fixed bottleneck conditions. The claim is nondirectional and the scope is limited to a controlled emulation; no generalization to real Internet users is implied.
proposal.question: Under fixed emulated bottleneck conditions, does adding 20 ms delay produce a measurable difference in TCP flow completion time compared to a 0 ms baseline?
proposal.hypothesis: Under fixed emulated bottleneck conditions, adding 20 ms delay changes TCP flow completion time.
proposal.conditions: Two conditions: (A) baseline — 0 ms client delay; (B) treatment — 20 ms client delay. All other bottleneck parameters held constant across conditions.
proposal.related_work: No full-text source was provided; the claim is described as synthetic. No prior measurements or citations are available to review.
proposal.alternatives: Observed differences could arise from TCP slow-start interactions with RTT, bufferbloat effects at the bottleneck, or CCA-specific window-growth behavior rather than delay alone. These mechanisms are untested alternatives.
proposal.design: Pilot emulated experiment comparing flow completion time (ms) between 0 ms and 20 ms delay conditions using a netem-based runner. Replications provide repeated observations per condition; a within-experiment comparison is used. A single completed trial cannot establish causality or generalize beyond the specific emulated topology.
proposal.metrics: Primary metric: flow_completion_time_ms (ms) per client per replication. Comparison: distribution of completion times under 0 ms vs. 20 ms delay.
proposal.controls: Bottleneck rate, buffer size, file size, CCA, loss rate, and number of clients are held constant. Only client delay varies between conditions.
proposal.falsification: The claim is falsified (no detectable change) if the distributions of flow completion time under 0 ms and 20 ms delay overlap substantially and a pre-specified statistical test (e.g., Mann-Whitney U, α=0.05) fails to reject the null of no difference. The claim is not falsified by a single trial alone.
proposal.inputs: Required but unresolved: runner script identity and version hash, bottleneck rate (Mbit/s), buffer size (kbytes), file size(s) (MBytes), CCA(s), client count, and delay placement (one-way vs. round-trip). Source SHA256 is synthetic placeholder (aaaa…); packet SHA256 is a1b401caab0920ee2f11377b7285ff0ef7269c187cfa7f3df1c1cb576ba8c0da.
proposal.limitations: A single emulated pilot cannot prove causality, cannot generalize to all Internet users, and cannot confirm the direction of the effect. Emulation differs from real-world Internet conditions. The claim is nondirectional; observing an increase does not fully validate it. Protocol is null pending resolution of script, topology, and delay-placement questions.
